lesson.title: Anchors and fast thinking

steps.headline: An anchor is a number you meet first, and it pulls later estimates towards it even when it is plainly irrelevant.

lead.text: Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to stop at 10 or 65. They then asked what percentage of United Nations members were African countries. Those who saw the higher number guessed higher.
Anchoring bias is the pull of a starting number on an estimate, even a number known to be random.
After the wheel stopped on 10, the median estimate was 25%. After it stopped on 65, the median estimate was 45%.

reveal.text: The number was plainly irrelevant, yet it moved the typical estimate by that gap.

model.quantity: Share of UN members that are African countries (%)
Estimated age of an oak tree (years)

steps.headline: The anchoring index divides the gap between median estimates by the gap between anchors.

lead.text: An index of 0 means the anchor was ignored. An index of 1 means estimates moved as far as the anchors did. Anchors of 0 and 100 with medians of 30 and 50 give 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2.
The index measures how much of the anchors' gap shows up in the estimates.

steps.headline: Find the anchoring index for anchors of 10 and 70 with median estimates of 30 and 51.

lesson.orientation: Measure the pull of an anchor and the bias of availability, then check a fast intuition with a slow one.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: One shop shows a jacket as “was £200, now £120”. Another shop sells the same jacket at £120, with no other price shown.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how far an anchor pulls an estimate, and see how ease of recall and quick answers can mislead.

recap.keyIdea: The first number you meet pulls your estimate, and what comes to mind easily feels common. Fast intuition is often right, so the skill is checking it when the stakes call for it.

blocks.text: You found that a random wheel moved median estimates by 20 points, an anchoring index of 0.4 for the tree ages, and that only a third of k-words start with k. The bat and ball cost 5p, not the 10p that springs to mind.

recap.nextHook: Fast thinking is shaped by what is in front of us. Next: how other people's behaviour shapes our own.

questions.prompt: After several news reports of shark attacks, a swimmer judges sharks a bigger risk than drowning. Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind is which heuristic?

questions.prompt: A pen and a notebook cost £2.20 together. The notebook costs £2.00 more than the pen. How much does the pen cost, in pence?
hints: Write the notebook's price in terms of the pen's.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer that springs to mind. Check it: the notebook would then cost £2.20 alone.

citations.claim: An anchor is a number you meet first, and it pulls later estimates towards it even when it is plainly irrelevant. Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to stop at 10 or 65. They then asked what percentage of United Nations members were African countries. Those who saw the higher number guessed higher. Anchoring bias is the pull of a starting number on an estimate, even a number known to be random.
After the wheel stopped on 10, the median estimate was 25%. After it stopped on 65, the median estimate was 45%. The number was plainly irrelevant, yet it moved the typical estimate by that gap.

The anchoring index divides the gap between median estimates by the gap between anchors. An index of 0 means the anchor was ignored. An index of 1 means estimates moved as far as the anchors did. Anchors of 0 and 100 with medians of 30 and 50 give 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2. The index measures how much of the anchors' gap shows up in the estimates.

Find the anchoring index for anchors of 10 and 70 with median estimates of 30 and 51. Find the gap between the medians. 51 − 30 = 21 Find the gap between the anchors. 70 − 10 = 60 Divide the first gap by the second. 21 ÷ 60 = 0.35

Anchors of 20 and 80 were used, and the median estimates of an oak tree's age were 35 and 59 years. Estimates moved 0.4 of the way between the anchors. Even random starting numbers pull estimates a long way.

Words with k third are about twice as common, yet words that start with k are easier to call to mind. Judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind is the availability heuristic.

Anchors of 100 and 500 produce median estimates of 220 and 340. What is the anchoring index? (340 − 220)/(500 − 100) = 120/400 = 0.3.
